headline: Bass crash the Execution Rocks as Sound water hits 68 — bunker schools trigger feeding frenzy
subhead: Outgoing tide at the lighthouse producing slot fish on live peanuts and bucktails.
body_markdown:
The Western Sound finally woke up this week, and it happened exactly where I knew it would — Execution Rocks on the outgoing tide. Water temperature hit 68 degrees across the Sound, that magic number that gets bass moving from their spring haunts into summer feeding mode. The temperature gradient between the bay water at 74 and the Sound proper at 68 is creating a feeding highway, and the bass are using it.

I've been watching this pattern for three decades. When bay water runs 6 degrees warmer than the Sound, it pushes bait out on every ebb tide. The peanut bunker that have been stacked in Little Neck Bay and Manhasset Bay all month are finally getting flushed into the main stem, and the bass are waiting for them at every choke point. Execution Rocks, Stepping Stones, the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings — anywhere current has to squeeze through structure, that's where you want to be.

The bite is happening on the start of the outgoing tide, right when the bay water begins its push toward the East River. I'm seeing guys do well with live peanuts on fishfinder rigs, 3/0 circle hooks, 20-pound fluorocarbon leaders. The key is getting that bait down in the current seam where the warm bay water meets the cooler Sound water. Fish are holding in 25 to 35 feet, right on the thermocline.

For artificials, white bucktails with 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullets are producing. Three-quarter ounce heads seem to be the sweet spot — heavy enough to get down in the current but light enough to work with the drift. I'm hearing reports of guys doing well on chartreuse and pink combinations too, especially when the water gets a little dirty from all this southwest wind we've been getting.

The Stepping Stones area has been consistent for slot fish in the 28 to 32-inch range. The current breaks around that lighthouse create perfect ambush points, and with the moon waning toward new, the tides are getting stronger every day. That's pushing more bait through the system and concentrating the bass in predictable spots.

Matinecock Point has been producing too, especially the deeper water off the point where it drops from 20 to 40 feet. The bass are using that depth change as a feeding station, picking off bunker that get disoriented in the current. Guys are doing well trolling small bunker spoons and mojos along that depth contour, but the live bait bite has been more consistent.

The southwest wind pattern we've had for the past week is actually helping the fishing. It's pushing surface water toward shore and creating an upwelling effect that brings cooler, oxygen-rich water up from the depths. That's why the water temperature has stabilized at 68 instead of continuing to climb — and bass love that stability.

Porgies are thick around Hart Island and the Stepping Stones. Nothing huge, but plenty of keeper-sized fish in the 10 to 12-inch range. High-low rigs with size 6 hooks and small pieces of clam or squid are all you need. The bite is best on the slack tides when the current isn't ripping.

Fluke fishing has been spotty but improving. The better fish are coming from the deeper water off Matinecock and around the Execution Rocks area. Guys are finding them in 30 to 40 feet on the edges of the channels. White Gulp and chartreuse bucktails are producing, but you need to work them slow. The fluke are still sluggish from the cooler spring we had.

Looking ahead, we've got a new moon on Friday, which means spring tides and stronger currents. That should really fire up the bass bite as more bait gets pushed through the system. The weather pattern looks stable through the weekend — southwest winds 10 to 15 knots, which is perfect for fishing the north shore structure. Water temperature should hold steady in the upper 60s, right in that sweet spot for summer bass fishing.

The key this week is timing your trips with the tide. The outgoing has been the producer, especially the first two hours of the ebb. Get to your spots early and be ready when that bay water starts moving. The bass are there — you just need to be in the right place when the dinner bell rings.
